items.title: Python 3.15.0 ships tomorrow (Oct 9) after a one-week slip — explicit lazy imports (PEP 810), the Tachyon sampling profiler (PEP 799), UTF-8 as default encoding (PEP 686), a new frozendict (PEP 814) and a 3–4% JIT improvement are in; macOS 27.0 users should wait for 3.15.1 because tkinter apps and IDLE hang
items.summary: Python 3.15.0 is now scheduled for final release on **October 9, 2026** — the stable launch slipped one week from the original October 1 target after last-minute lazy-import bugs forced a surprise third release candidate. 3.15.0rc3 shipped on October 2 with roughly 156 bugfixes, build improvements and documentation changes from 82 contributors since rc2. The release manager cited specific lazy-import blockers as the reason: one bug was that `lazy import a.b as c` was treating `b` as an attribute of `a` instead of importing the `a.b` submodule. The release notes confirm there are no ABI changes from rc2 onward, so wheels built against the release candidates will keep working with later 3.15 versions. **Headline features landing in 3.15**: (1) **PEP 810 — Explicit lazy imports** — a new `lazy` keyword (`lazy import json`) that creates a proxy object, defers loading until first use, and lists the module in `sys.lazy_modules` rather than `sys.modules`. The target use cases are CLI tools, test suites and large dependency graphs where startup cost dominates. (2) **PEP 814 — frozendict** as a built-in type. (3) **PEP 661 — Sentinel** type for the stdlib. (4) **PEP 799 — Tachyon sampling profiler** as a dedicated stdlib `profiling` package (new high-frequency, low-overhead statistical sampling profiler per the alpha notes). (5) **PEP 686 — UTF-8 as the default encoding**. (6) **PEP 798 — unpacking in comprehensions**, plus improved error messages. (7) **JIT upgrade** with a reported 3–4% geometric-mean performance improvement on x86-64 Linux. **Known issue flagged in rc3 coverage**: tkinter applications including IDLE can hang on macOS 27.0 — a specific day-one blocker for anyone on the newest macOS release, pointing to a wait for 3.15.1. Instagram's internal production figures for lazy imports (widely cited but not primary-source-confirmed) are 50–80% startup time reductions and 40–90% memory reductions; lazy imports speed up startup, not steady-state execution.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: this is directly on-stack and the kind of release-eve moment where the practical details are the whole value. Four concrete things worth filing before you hit `brew upgrade python@3.15` or `pyenv install 3.15.0` tomorrow. First, **explicit lazy imports are the one feature that changes how you write Python scripts in a hobby context**. `lazy import json` creates a proxy object and the module isn't actually loaded until the first attribute access — which means a script that imports pandas/numpy/requests at the top just-in-case now has a near-zero cold-start cost for the paths that never touch them. For a CLI tool or a quick data-wrangling script, the real unlock is you can keep `import pandas as pd` at the top of the file and get `--help` to render in milliseconds instead of seconds. The gotcha the PEP discussion surfaced: if a lazy import fails on first use, the proxy isn't replaced, so the next access retries — not a persistent error, just a 'why does this sometimes work on retry' bug if you don't know to look for it. Second, **the macOS 27.0 + tkinter hang warning is the immediate day-one footgun**. If you're on macOS 27.0 and you use IDLE or any tkinter-based app, upgrading to 3.15.0 on launch day will hang on you. The right move: wait for 3.15.1 (first bugfix release, usually ~6 weeks later) or stay on 3.14 until the issue has a confirmed fix in a point release. Third, **the Tachyon sampling profiler ships as a stdlib package** — this is the first time Python has had a sampling profiler in the standard library (cProfile is deterministic, which adds overhead). For a hobbyist who's been reaching for `py-spy` or `scalene` when a script runs slower than expected, the practical read: for a lot of casual profiling needs, you now get a lower-friction baseline without the external install dance. Fourth, **UTF-8 as the default encoding (PEP 686) is the quiet one that fixes a specific class of 'why does my script work on my laptop but break on CI' bug** — the ones where a `open('file.txt')` call on Windows was falling through to cp1252 and corrupting non-ASCII content. If you've ever hit a `UnicodeDecodeError` on a CSV or JSON file after moving code between machines, this is the fix. Practical concrete next step: **don't upgrade production hobby workloads tomorrow — wait a week for ecosystem catchup on the big libraries (pandas, numpy, requests, cryptography) to confirm 3.15 wheel availability**. If you're on macOS 27.0 and use IDLE, wait for 3.15.1 outright. For a fresh project where you want to try `lazy import`, create a `pyenv install 3.15.0` sandbox tomorrow afternoon and see how a CLI tool's startup time looks before and after.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Python 3.15.0 ships tomorrow after a one-week lazy-import-bug slip — explicit lazy imports, a stdlib sampling profiler and UTF-8 as default are the headline features, but macOS 27.0 users should wait for 3.15.1 to avoid tkinter/IDLE hangs.

takes.take: Primary source — confirms Oct 9 2026 final target, ABI stability from rc2 onward, and standard 'release candidate, not for production' advisory.
Specifies the one-week slip from Oct 1 to Oct 9 and names the lazy-import blockers as the delay reason. Flags the macOS 27.0 tkinter/IDLE hang as a known day-one issue.

Covers the specific lazy-import bug (`lazy import a.b as c` treating `b` as an attribute of `a` instead of importing the submodule) that caused the slip, and the 156-bugfix / 82-contributor delta between rc2 and rc3.

Primary source for the lazy-imports feature — Steering Council acceptance dated Nov 3 2025, keyword syntax (`lazy import json`), proxy-object semantics, `sys.lazy_modules` listing. Flags that if a lazy import fails on first use, the proxy is not replaced and the next use retries.

takes.source: JetBrains PyCharm blog — Explicit lazy imports are coming to Python 3.15
takes.take: Developer-facing walkthrough of lazy imports — explains the proxy mechanic, the `sys.lazy_modules` listing, the retry-on-failure semantic, and open compatibility-shim concerns for libraries supporting both 3.14 and 3.15.
